title: Love peace, pursue peace (Avot 1:12)
hookLine: Hillel: be a disciple of Aaron, loving peace, loving people, drawing them near
last: HALF A WAGE, JUST TO LISTEN.

lines: PICK A SIDE, OR STAY OUT?
cards: Two friends have stopped talking. Maybe it was a wedding seating chart, maybe money, maybe one sharp text. You're friends with both, and you know the silence is hurting them both.

The usual moves are two: pick a side, or carefully stay out of it. Pirkei Avot now reaches the poor laborer from the roof, all grown up. He's the last of the great pairs in the chain, alongside a sage named Shammai.
And his first saying is about exactly this moment: two people who won't speak, and someone in the middle.

teach.b: Hillel came to the land of Israel from Babylonia, poor and hungry to learn, and later tradition remembers him for his patience.
His saying begins: be one of the disciples of Aaron, Moses's brother, the high priest. What kind of disciple?
Loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and drawing them near to the Torah. Why Aaron? The Torah never tells a story of Aaron making peace.

The rabbis filled that silence. An early collection called Avot of Rabbi Natan says that when two people quarreled, Aaron would sit with one of them and say, your friend is heartbroken, he's ashamed of what he did to you.
Then he would go to the other and say the same thing. And when the two met, they would embrace. Notice the verbs.
Loving peace is a feeling. Pursuing peace is a chase. The Hebrew word is rodef, the word for running after something.
Hillel may be echoing a psalm, which in the old Jewish Publication Society translation says, "Depart from evil, and do good; Seek peace, and pursue it." Peace doesn't come looking for you.
You go after it, like Aaron walking from one house to the other.
Then the last part: love people, and draw them near.
Hillel's word means all creatures, every human being, not only the ones who already agree with you. He doesn't say push them toward the Torah. He says bring them close.
A disciple of Aaron walks between people until they can find each other again.

how: Aaron is held up in Jewish teaching as the model peacemaker, and the Mishnah counts making peace between people (hava'at shalom) among the good deeds whose fruits a person enjoys in this world.

o: a psalm-writer who said seek peace and pursue it
the sage from Babylonia who said to pursue peace
the high priest, Moses's brother, who made peace

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah tells how Aaron made peace between quarreling friends
the Torah is silent. the story comes from the rabbis, in Avot of Rabbi Natan.
Hillel says to pursue peace, not only love it
loving peace and pursuing peace: the second is a chase.
Hillel said to draw near only people who already study Torah
he said love all people, every creature, and bring them close.

games.q: you're Aaron. two friends have quarreled and won't speak. what do you do?
o: tell them both they're being childish.
go to each and tell them the other is sorry.
stay out of it. it's their business.
games.why: the rabbis say Aaron sat with each one and said your friend is heartbroken over this, until the two met and embraced.

practice: Think of two people in your life who aren't getting along, family, coworkers, friends, and remember something good about each of them.
Then ask what one small, true thing you could say to either one that would make the other seem a little more human: one sentence, like Aaron's. If you pray, you can hold them both before God.

wordCard.voice: Hillel. The sage from Babylonia who said: be a disciple of Aaron, love peace and chase it, love people and draw them near.

orig.note: Hebrew: pursuing peace. Hillel's words for Aaron's way (Avot 1:12).

carryVoice: Your line: pursue peace. Loving it is only the first half. Day two hundred forty-three.
